title: The Ethiopian Canon - Part 1
subtitle: Start Here: How to Use This Book, the Reader's Charter, and the Prologue
description:
Open almost any Bible and turn past the title page. Before Genesis there is a page most of us have never read on purpose: the table of contents.

This is Start Here, the opening part of The Ethiopian Canon: What It Contains and Why It Matters. It gathers everything that comes before the main chapters, so you can see how the book is built, what it promises and whether it is for you before you go further.

Inside this part

  • How to Use This Book — how to read the book straight through, and how to open it again as a reference.
  • A Note on Names, Numbers, and Sources — how the book spells Ethiopian names, writes Ge’ez and cites its sources.
  • The Reader’s Charter — the book’s four claims, written as what each one gives you, with the chapters where each is earned.
  • Prologue: A Question in the Table of Contents — sets the familiar sixty-six-book list beside the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church’s own list, and states the book’s claim in four foundations: the right to ask, Africa as maker, our own tradition of reading Ethiopia, and a practice we can pass on.

An honest edition

This is an independent work of study. It is not an official publication of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church or of any other church body, and it does not speak for them. Scripture quotations are from the King James Version, and the Church’s own list of books is quoted from its English-language website.

Digital edition (PDF), 22 pages. Instant access from your Account page after purchase. This is part 1 of 5 of a 395-page volume (pages 8–22 of the complete book, plus cover and front matter). The complete volume is also sold separately as The Ethiopian Canon - Full Version.
what_you_learn: How the book is built, and how to read it straight through or use it as a reference
How the book spells and explains Ethiopian names such as Ge'ez, Aksum, Tewahedo and Meqabyan
Why the table of contents in your Bible is a question worth asking
The four foundations the whole book builds on
Where each of the other parts fits, and where to begin if you start in the middle
who_for:
• Bible readers who noticed that the table of contents is not the same in every church and want a clear, calm, honest explanation.
  • Black Christians and readers of African heritage who want to understand Ethiopia’s place in the history of Scripture.
  • Pastors, Sunday school teachers and small-group leaders looking for a sourced resource.
  • Curious readers who have seen viral videos about “hidden books of the Bible” and want to separate fact from hype.
  • Readers who want to see how the book argues before they buy the longer parts.

No background in Hebrew, Greek or Ge’ez is needed. No one is asked to give up their own Bible.

title: The Ethiopian Canon - Part 2
subtitle: Booklet 1 of 3: The Bible We Inherited, and How Ethiopia Carried Scripture
description:
Who gave us the table of contents we trust, and what happens when we learn it has a history?

This part holds Parts One and Two of The Ethiopian Canon (Chapters 1–9). Part One looks at the sixty-six-book Bible that many Black American families and congregations received. Part Two travels to the Ethiopian highlands to see how an African church kept, copied and explained Scripture.

Inside this part

  • Part One: The Bible We Inherited — “The Bible Many of Us Were Given,” “Who Gives a Table of Contents Authority?”, “How Sixty-Six Became Our Familiar Number” and “Why Ethiopia Was Already in Our Imagination.”
  • Part Two: How Ethiopia Carried Scripture — “Aksum and an African Christian Center,” “When Scripture Lived in Ge’ez,” “The Hands That Kept the Pages,” “A Church That Explained What It Read” and “From a Living Church to the Printed Bible.”
  • Questions to carry — each part opens with a question to take into it.

An honest edition

This is an independent work of study. It is not an official publication of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church or of any other church body, and it does not speak for them. Scripture quotations are from the King James Version, and the Church’s own list of books is quoted from its English-language website.

Digital edition (PDF), 116 pages. Instant access from your Account page after purchase. This is part 2 of 5 of a 395-page volume (pages 23–132 of the complete book, plus cover and front matter). The complete volume is also sold separately as The Ethiopian Canon - Full Version.

How church teachers explained what they read, and the road from a living church to the printed Bible

title: The Ethiopian Canon - Part 3
subtitle: Booklet 2 of 3: What Eighty-One Holds, and How Texts Become Visible or Invisible
description:
What is actually on the Ethiopian list, and why does the number 81 turn out to be more interesting than a sum?

This part holds Parts Three and Four of The Ethiopian Canon (Chapters 10–20). Part Three is the map of the Ethiopian list, book by book. Part Four asks a better question than “Who hid the books?”: by what steps does a text become visible to a reader, or disappear from view?

Inside this part

  • Part Three: What Eighty-One Holds — how the Ethiopian church counts to eighty-one, the familiar Old Testament in a wider house, Enoch and Jubilees, Meqabyan as its own story, the books whose names we have barely learned, the New Testament’s wider door, and the books beside the Bible.
  • Part Four: How Texts Become Visible or Invisible — four histories (lost, removed, hidden, preserved), what a fragment can tell us, “The English Book in Your Hands,” and “Who Made Scripture Reach Us?”

An honest edition

This is an independent work of study. It is not an official publication of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church or of any other church body, and it does not speak for them. Scripture quotations are from the King James Version, and the Church’s own list of books is quoted from its English-language website.

Digital edition (PDF), 128 pages. Instant access from your Account page after purchase. This is part 3 of 5 of a 395-page volume (pages 133–254 of the complete book, plus cover and front matter). The complete volume is also sold separately as The Ethiopian Canon - Full Version.

title: The Ethiopian Canon - Part 4
subtitle: Booklet 3 of 3: Ethiopia and the Black Reader, and the Reader Who Can Pass It On
description:
What happens when the Ethiopia of Black American hope meets the Ethiopian church and its books, and what do we owe each other?

This part holds Parts Five and Six of The Ethiopian Canon with the Epilogue (Chapters 21–27). By Part Five the book’s four foundations are laid; this part tests them, lets them speak to one another, and ends with tools instead of a summary.

Inside this part

  • Part Five: Ethiopia and the Black Reader — Black American poems and anthems of “Ethiopia” read line by line beside the Ethiopian church’s own words, a conversation across Black Christian traditions, the African hands behind Christian knowledge, an hour of reading across canons at one table, and “What We Mean by an African Foundation.”
  • Part Six: The Reader Who Can Pass It On — a method for testing the next claim you hear about the Ethiopian Bible, and a plan for a small library and a practice of reading to share with family, congregation and community.
  • Epilogue: Open the Book Again — a last invitation to open the Bible you were given once more.

An honest edition

This is an independent work of study. It is not an official publication of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church or of any other church body, and it does not speak for them. Scripture quotations are from the King James Version, and the Church’s own list of books is quoted from its English-language website.

Digital edition (PDF), 84 pages. Instant access from your Account page after purchase. This is part 4 of 5 of a 395-page volume (pages 255–332 of the complete book, plus cover and front matter). The complete volume is also sold separately as The Ethiopian Canon - Full Version.

title: The Ethiopian Canon - Part 5
subtitle: Back Matter: Appendices, Glossary, Bibliography, and Index
description:
The reference shelf of The Ethiopian Canon: the atlas, the book guide, the timeline and the ledger of every claim.

This part holds everything that comes after the Epilogue of The Ethiopian Canon. It is a reference booklet: its entries point back to chapters and pages in the other parts, so it is most useful beside the main text.

Inside this part

  • Appendix A: The Canon Atlas — the Church’s own list of eighty-one, set beside the other ways the number has been recorded.
  • Appendix B: Book Guide, A to Z — the books you have least likely heard of.
  • Appendix C: A Timeline from Aksum to Harlem — the Ethiopian Scriptures beside the English Bible in Black America.
  • Appendix D: Edition Checklist — five questions to ask of any English book that calls itself an “Ethiopian Bible.”
  • Appendix E: The Foundation Ledger — every brick of the book’s argument with its source, so you can test the structure yourself.
  • Glossary, Bibliography and Index — terms, sources and a page-number index for the complete volume.

An honest edition

This is an independent work of study. It is not an official publication of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church or of any other church body, and it does not speak for them. Scripture quotations are from the King James Version, and the Church’s own list of books is quoted from its English-language website.

Digital edition (PDF), 69 pages. Instant access from your Account page after purchase. This is part 5 of 5 of a 395-page volume (pages 333–395 of the complete book, plus cover and front matter). The complete volume is also sold separately as The Ethiopian Canon - Full Version.
